title: Single-Phase Center-Tapped Transformer
summary: An Electric Machines design-and-fabrication project connecting winding calculations with bobbin availability, core fit and practical redesign.
overview: The report documents a 220 V primary and a 380 V secondary design with a 220 V tap, using an E-I laminated core. It connects core area, turns per volt, winding turns, current ratings and wire-gauge selection with fabrication. The project retains its original center-tapped title; the documented tap voltages do not establish equal secondary halves or measured output ratings.
approach: Translated the academic load/voltage brief into core and winding calculations, including turns per volt, primary/secondary turns, currents and wire-gauge requirements.
The initial handwritten calculation used 57 VA with a 220 V primary and a 380 V secondary with a 220 V tap. This is an initial design calculation, not a verified hardware nameplate.
The report describes difficulty sourcing the first bobbin and fitting the core after winding. The team moved to a larger bobbin and recalculated the arrangement.

A later handwritten page records an apparent-power calculation of about 210 VA for the larger bobbin, retaining the documented primary, secondary and tap voltages. This is a separate design iteration.
Wound and insulated the coils, assembled the E-I core and mounting hardware, and included open-/short-circuit test work in the project scope.
outcomes: Fabricated the transformer shown in the hardware photograph and documented a redesign around winding/core fit.
The owner caption reports test work, but measured voltages, efficiency, regulation and test values are not established by the supplied report.
The documented 380 V secondary with a 220 V tap describes the design arrangement, not a verified output specification or equal secondary halves.

evidenceNotes: Phase-2 visual review of handwritten report pages 11 and 13 confirms 220 V primary, 380 V secondary and a 220 V tap. The original center-tapped project title is retained; mathematically equal secondary halves are not claimed.
The initial calculation uses 57 VA; the larger-bobbin calculation is approximately 210 VA. Neither establishes a measured rating of the fabricated hardware.
Report page 12 describes bobbin sourcing and winding/core-fit difficulties. Avoid repeating its weak wire-gauge/turn-count causality as a general engineering rule.
Report page 14 has an open/short-circuit test heading but no recorded measurements. The owner-supplied caption supports test work, not numerical efficiency/regulation/test results.
Report cover establishes team names and course context, without individual contributions. Student identifiers are excluded.
General supporting power-grid diagram voltages are not fabricated-device ratings.
Photograph winding-label names and identifiers were sanitized in the public copy.
problem: Design and fabricate a single-phase transformer for an academic power-plant control-room brief, working from a 220 V primary and required secondary/tap voltages.
context: An Electric Machines Lab Complex Engineering Activity at Air University, Spring 2025. Team calculations and the fabricated hardware document the work.
constraints: Bobbin availability and the space required by the windings affected whether the laminated core could be fitted.
The 57 VA and approximately 210 VA calculations belong to different design iterations; neither is presented as a measured rating of the photographed transformer.
The supplied report has an open-/short-circuit-test page without recorded measurements.
lessons: A winding calculation must fit a real bobbin and core assembly; material availability and fabrication geometry can force a new calculation.
Design iterations and measured results need separate records so a calculated apparent-power value is not mistaken for verified hardware performance.
nextSteps: A fuller technical record would require measured secondary/tap voltages and the original open-/short-circuit readings before assigning performance or a tested rating.
